# define the gravitational constant
G = 6.67e-11 # m**3 kg / s

def magnitude(a):
    '''
    This function returns the magnitude of a vector.
    
    Parmeters
    ---------
    a : numpy array
        An array representing a physical vector.
        It can have any number of elements,
        but 2 or 3 elements will be most common:
            in 2D, a = np.array([x, y])
            in 3D, a = np.array([x, y, z])

    Returns
    -------
    |a| : float
        The magnitude (length) of the array.
    '''

    return np.sqrt(np.sum(a**2))

def unit(a):
    '''
    This function returns a vector's unit vector
    (the vector that is parallel to it but has length of 1)
    
    Parmeters
    ---------
    a : numpy array
        An array representing a physical vector.
        It can have any number of elements,
        but 2 or 3 elements will be most common:
            in 2D, a = np.array([x, y])
            in 3D, a = np.array([x, y, z])

    Returns
    -------
    a_hat : float
        The unit vector parallel to the vector
    '''

    return a/magnitude(a)

def separation(p_i, p_j):
    '''
    This function returns the separation between two vectors.
    
    Parmeters
    ---------
    p_i : numpy array
        An array representing a physical vector.
    
    p_j : numpy array
        An array representing a second physical vector.

    Returns
    -------
    r_ij : numpy array
        The separation vector, p_j - p_i.
    '''

    return p_j - p_i
    
def force_magnitude(m_i, m_j, r):
    '''
    This function returns the magnitude of the 
    gravitational force, given two masses
    and a separation.
    
    Parmeters
    ---------
    m_i : float
        A mass, in kg.
    
    m_j : float
        A mass, in kg.
        
    r : float
        The distance between the two masses, in kg.

    Returns
    -------
    F_g : float
        The magnitude of the force of gravity between them, in N.
    '''

    return (G*m_i*m_j)/(r**2)

def forceVector(m_i, m_j, p_i, p_j):
    '''
    This function returns the full gravitational force vector
    for the force acting on particle i, caused by particle j.
    


    Parmeters
    ---------
    m_i : float
        A mass representing particle i, in kg.
    
    m_j : float
        A mass representing particle j, in kg.
        
    p_i : numpy array
        A vector representing the position of particle i.
    
    p_j : numpy array
        A vector representing the position of particle j.


    Returns
    -------
    F_g : numpy array
        The force vector acting on particle i, in N.
    '''
    
    # calculate the separation vector, and its magnitude
    r_vector = separation(p_i, p_j)
    r_magnitude = magnitude(r_vector)
    #print(f" the seperation is, {r_vector}")
    # calculate the magnitude of the force
    F_magnitude = force_magnitude(m_i, m_j, r_magnitude)

    # calculate the direction of the force, as a unit vector
    F_unit = unit(r_vector)
    
    # return the full force vector
    return F_magnitude * F_unit

def netForces(masses, positions):
    """
    Compute net gravitational force vector exerted on 
    particle i by all particles j, and do this for all i.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    masses : list of floats
        Particle masses in kg.
    positions : list of numpy arrays
        Particle positions in cartesian coordinates in m.
        
    Returns
    -------
    netForces : list of numpy arrays
        Components of gravitational force vectors in N.
        
    Example
    -------
    >>> # forces between Earth and 70 kg person on surface
    >>> masses = [6e24,70]
    >>> radiusEarth = 6380000 # m
    >>> positions = [np.array([0, 0, 0])*radiusEarth, np.array([1, 1, 1])*radiusEarth]
    >>> netForces(masses,positions)
    [array([   0.        ,    0.        ,  688.23026503]),
     array([   0.        ,    0.        , -688.23026503])]
    
    """
    # empty force list
    force_list = []
    
    # for each body i
    for i in range(len(masses)):

        # zero net force vector; add to this for each j
        net_force_i = np.zeros(3)

        # vector sum all forces on i by bodies j
        for j in range(len(masses)):
            # omit self-interactions (body i on itself):
            if i != j:  
                # vector sum of net force with additional force from body j
                net_force_i += forceVector(masses[i],masses[j],positions[i],positions[j])

        # add net force to force list:
        force_list.append(net_force_i)
        
    return force_list

def plotParticles2WithQuivers(masses, positions, forces):
    xPositions = []
    yPositions = []
    xForces = []
    yForces = []
    for i in range(len(masses)):
        xPositions.append(positions[i][0]/au)
        yPositions.append(positions[i][1]/au)
        xForces.append(forces[i][0])
        yForces.append(forces[i][1])

    areaForSymbol = masses/np.max(masses)*100
    plt.scatter(xPositions,yPositions, s=areaForSymbol)
    plt.quiver(xPositions,yPositions,xForces,yForces)

    plt.axis('scaled')
    plt.xlabel('X (AU)')
    plt.ylabel('Y (AU)')

Ok, so using a few of the functions from homework D, I can calculate a list of 3-dimensional force vectors from a list of 3-dimensional positions, a list of masses and a list of separations.

2 leapfrog integrator¶

Leapfrog integratioon formula¶

$$ r_{i}(t+\Delta t) = r_{i}(t)+v_{i}(t)(\Delta t)+ 1/2a_{i}(t)(\Delta t)^2$$ $$ v_{i}(t+\Delta t) = v_{i}(t)+1/2[a_{i}(t)+a_{i}(t+\Delta t)](\Delta t)$$ $$ a_{i}(t+\Delta t) = \frac{F_{i}(t+\Delta t)}{m_{i}} $$

In [60]:
#leapfrog function
def leapfrogStep(r_i, v_i, F, masses, delta_t, display):
    '''
    Calculate the position of a particle
    given the force, initial position r_i,
    initial velocity, Force on the particle and 
    the time step between start_t and end_t

    -----inputs-----------------

    *All inputs are for the same one spatial dimension

    r_i: float or integer 
    The initial position of the particle in one dimension 
    r_i has units of meters

    v_i: float or integer
    The initial velocity of the particle in one dimension
    v_i has units of meters per second

    a_i: float or integer
    The initial acceleration of the particle in one dimension
    a_i has units of meters per second squared

    F: function
    a function that describes the force at every time interval for the particle in one dimension
    f has units of newtons

    display: boolean
    the display boolean will tell if the function should print the values or just return them 
    
    -------------function------------

    the leapstep function calculates the new velocities for one delta time

    -----output-------------

    The lestep function outputs

    
    '''
    #assigning all of the inputs in the functions as variables insiee the function
    
    
    
    
    
    a_i = F(masses, r_i) #my function returns the acceleration

    r_i = np.array(r_i)

    v_i = np.array(v_i)
    
    r_t = r_i+v_i*delta_t+1/2*(a_i)*delta_t**2

    a_t = F( masses, r_t) #my function returns the acceleration

    v_t = v_i+1/2*(a_i + a_t)*delta_t

    if display == True:
        print(f" a = {a_t} v = {v_t} r = {r_t}")
        return( a_t, v_t, r_t)
    else:
        return( a_t, v_t, r_t)
    

    
    current_t += delta_t #incrementing current_t by delta_t

YESSSSS! The code I just ran in the code cell above! This demonstrates that both my fixed leapfrogStep function and my force function are working correctly! I simulated what would happen to a person such as myself standing 1 Earth radius away from the center of the Earth at rest, and my functions calculated that the person would accelerate down towards the center of the Earth at 9.79 meters per second squared! The Earth would barely accelerate up. The velocity after 1 second would be 0.70 meters per second down, and the position would be a little closer together!

3 Write a function called calculateTrajectories¶

For this, I will simply rewrite the for loop in my current leapfrogStep function to remove it. I will then rewrite that for loop into a function called calculateTrajectories. The calculateTrajectories function will have the outputs:

1 times (1D array, with elements identifying each time step)
2 positions at all times (multi-dimensional array or arrays)
3 velocities at all times (multi-dimensional array or arrays)

Your returned times, positions, and velocities arrays should all contain your initial time (t=0), positions, and velocities as well.

In [178]:
#leapfrog function
def calculateTrajectories(r_i, v_i, F, masses, delta_t, start_t, end_t, display):
    '''
    Calculate the position of a particle
    given the force, initial position r_i,
    initial velocity, Force on the particle and 
    the time step between start_t and end_t

    -----inputs-----------------

    *All inputs are for the same one spatial dimension

    r_i: a list of the initial positions of the particles
    r_i has units of meters

    v_i: a list of the initial velocities of the particles
    v_i has units of meters per second


    F: function
    a function that describes the force at every time interval for the particle in one dimension
    f has units of newtons

    delta_t: flaot
    The time increment you would like to subdivide the time period from start_time to end_time in

    start_t: float
    The time you would like to start calculating the trajectory of the particle at

    end_t: float
    The time you would like to end calculating the trajectory of the particle at
    
    display: boolean
    The display boolean will tell if the function should print the values or just return them 
    
    
    -----------what the function actualy does---------------

    The calculateTrajectories function will use the leapfrogStep function to calculate the 
    position, veelcoty and acceleration of each particle at each time, then add it to a list

    -----------output----------------

    if display == True then the function will print all of the positions, velocities, and accelerations in a
    nice f string

    if display == false then the function will just return the lists for position, velocity, and acceleration

    
    '''
    #assigning all of the inputs in the functions as variables insiee the function


    # making four global lists to store the times, positions, velocities and accelerations
    #print(type(F))
    global position
    position = [r_i]
    global velocity
    velocity = [v_i]
    global acceleration
    acceleration = [[[0,0,0], [0,0,0]]]
    masses = np.array(masses)
    r_i = np.array(r_i)
    

 
    global time
    time = [start_t]
    

 
    current_t = start_t
    v_t = v_i #setting the first veloecity v_t as the inital velovity v_i
    if display == True:
        while current_t <= end_t: #looping through all t including end_t
            if current_t == start_t:
                
                a_t, v_t, r_t = leapfrogStep(r_i, v_i, F, masses, delta_t, display)
                current_t += delta_t #incrementing current_t by delta_t
                position.append(r_t)
                velocity.append(v_t)
                acceleration.append(a_t)
                time.append(current_t)
            else:
                a_t, v_t, r_t = leapfrogStep(r_t, v_t, F, masses, delta_t, display)
                current_t += delta_t #incrementing current_t by delta_t
                position.append(r_t)
                velocity.append(v_t)
                acceleration.append(a_t)
                time.append(current_t)
        
        print(f"the final position is, {position[-1]}, the final velocity is, {v_t} meters/seocnd")

    else:
        while current_t <= end_t: #looping through all t including end_t
            
            if current_t == start_t: 
                a_t, v_t, r_t = leapfrogStep(r_i, v_i, F, masses, delta_t, display)
                current_t += delta_t #incrementing current_t by delta_t
                position.append(r_t)
                velocity.append(v_t)
                acceleration.append(a_t)
                time.append(current_t)
            else:
                a_t, v_t, r_t = leapfrogStep(r_t, v_t, F, masses, delta_t, display)
                current_t += delta_t #incrementing current_t by delta_t
                position.append(r_t)
                velocity.append(v_t)
                acceleration.append(a_t)
                time.append(current_t)

my calculateTrajectories function seems to be working with the test case of me falling towards the center of mass of the Earth.. My acceleration stayed relatively constant which makes sense for the time scale of 11 seconds

my acceleration started at -9.79203950e+00 m/s/s at time = 0 and ended at -9.79384380e+00 m/s/s at time = 11 However, it did increase in magnitude as time increased because I was getting closer to the center of the Earth This shows that I am successfully calling my force(masses, positions) function

Similarly, my velocity started at [0, 0, 0] m/s at time = 0 my velocity ended at [ 0.00000000e+00, -9.79252812e+01, 0.00000000e+00] m/s at time = 11 after ten seconds of free falll. This is the correct amount as velocity = acceleration*time and since the acceleration was nearly constant 9.79203950e+00 and only slightly increased, and I fell for 10 seconds, my final velocity should be slightly greater in magnitude than -97.920395 m/s. Since my final velocity is -97.9252812m/s, which is just slightly greater in order of magnitude than -97.920395 m/s, this is another good sign that both my leapfrogStep and my calculateTrajectories function are working correctly

Finally, my position started at [ 0, 6378137, 0] at time = 0 my position ended at [0.00000000e+00, 6.37754456e+06, 0.00000000e+00] at time = 11 This demonstrates again that both my leapfrogStep and my calculateTrajectories function are working correctly, as my ending position has a smaller y-value than my starting position, as I am moving towards the center of mass of the Earth.

5 Make three plots summarizing the results¶

the first plot should have time on the horizontal axis, and show the 𝑥 positions of both particles on the vertical axis. Estimate the period of orbit by eye; does this make sense?

the second plot should show the trajectories that the particles trace out in the 𝑥-𝑦 plane. The Earth’s orbit should be pretty close to a perfect circle. Scale the axes so it appears this way.

the third plot should show the 𝑥 velocity of the Sun as a function of time. Based on this plot, to what precision would we need to measure the radial velocity of a Sun-like star to see an Earth-like planet orbiting it? (Estimate this by eye.)

For all positions and times, convert back to AU and days for the above plots.

The Sun's x-velocity looks to be the derivative of the Earth's x-position. This would make sense as the Earth would pull on the sun, changing its velocity. Assuming the change in the Sun's x-velocity is caused solely by the inner terrestrial planets, we would need a telescope that can resolve centimeters from light-years away. This is becayse the variation of the sun's velocity is about 15 centimeters per/second(it has a minimum x velocity of -7.5centimeters/second and a maximum x velocity of about 7.5 centimeters per second). This would be extremely difficult for any modern telescope to resolve, as the closest star is about 4 light-years away, I believe, so resolving a difference of 15 centimeters would be nearly impossible at interstellar distances.

7 Read in the initial conditions describing the Kepler-16ABb circumbinary planet system¶

Stored in the file kepler16.txt on Canvas. The file contains 7 columns: one for masses, three for positions, and three for velocities. Read in the data file and organize these initial conditions into arrays that could be fed as inputs to your calculateTrajectories function

This is quite simple. I will read the files from Canvas, sort the data, and then input that data into my calculateTrajectories function

In [193]:
import pandas as pd # I'm going to use pandas to read the kepler-16.txt file
In [194]:
file = 'kepler16.txt'
row = 4

mass = [] #kg
x = [] #meters
y = [] #meters
z = [] #meters
vx = [] # m/s
vy = [] # m
vz = [] # m/s

for rows in range(row-1): #reading the data skipping over the first 8 rows of header


    single_row = pd.read_csv(file, skiprows=rows + 1, nrows=1, header=None) ##assinign a single row to this list
    #print(single_row[0][0])
    #print(single_row[0][0][72:83]) #checking to make sure the indices are correct
    
    
    #use slicing to get each value out that's separated by a space
    
    mass.append(single_row[0][0][0:11]) # assigning the first element of the row as the mass
    x.append(single_row[0][0][12:23]) #assigning the second element of the row to x(m)
    y.append(single_row[0][0][24:36]) #assigning the third element of the row to y(m)
    z.append(single_row[0][0][36:47]) #assigning the fourth element of the row to z(m)
    vx.append(single_row[0][0][48:59]) #assigning the second element of the row to vx(m/s)
    vy.append(single_row[0][0][60:71]) #assigning the third element of the row to vy(m/s)
    vz.append(single_row[0][0][72:83]) #assigning the fourth element of the row to vz(m/s)


# converting the list to numpy arrays

x = np.array(x)
y = np.array(y)

For this, I will make a 3d animation using what was covered in lecture 23

Below is the code from lecture 23

In [ ]:
#code I will base my 3d plotting off from lecture 23
from mpl_toolkits import mplot3d

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6,6))
ax = plt.axes(projection='3d')

ax.set_xlabel('x')
ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_zlabel('t')
ax.zaxis.labelpad=-2 # sets the z-axis label position

# Data for a three-dimensional line
tline = np.linspace(0, 15, 1000)
xline = np.sin(tline)
yline = np.cos(tline)
ax.plot(xline, yline, tline, 'gray')

# Data for three-dimensional scattered points
tdata = 15 * np.random.random(100)
tdata.sort()
xdata = np.sin(tdata) + 0.1 * np.random.randn(100)
ydata = np.cos(tdata) + 0.1 * np.random.randn(100)
ax.scatter(xdata, ydata, tdata, c=tdata, cmap='coolwarm')

import matplotlib.animation as ani
FFMpegWriter = ani.writers['ffmpeg']
writer = FFMpegWriter(fps=10)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7, 7))
fig.patch.set_alpha(1.0) # Python bug fix... still

# Write plots to frames of an animation
with writer.saving(fig, "ecc_vec.mp4", 150):
    
    for i in range(0,len(time_array)):
        
        plt.quiver([0, 0], [0, 0], position_array[i, :, 0], position_array[i, :, 1], color=["blue", "orange"], scale=1)

        plt.xlim(-0.4, 0.4); plt.ylim(-0.4, 0.4);
        plt.xlabel(r'$e_x$'); plt.ylabel(r'$e_y$');
        plt.title(f'Eccentricity Vector at time = {time_array[i]:02.2f}')

        writer.grab_frame()
        
        plt.cla()

help(planetesimalDisk)

Help on function planetesimalDisk in module systems:

planetesimalDisk(num_of_particles=30, mass_ratio=1e-10, z_velocity=1000.0)
    This function creates N-body initial conditions for a (very) cartoon
    model of a disk of planetesimals (baby planets) orbiting around the
    star.
    
    At very small values, the gravity is totally dominated by the central
    star. At larger values (above about 1e-6, roughly an Earth mass per
    particle), the orbits may start to go unstable due to the interactions
    between the particles.
    
    The disk will be created mostly in the x-y plane, but you can add
    random velocities with a standard deviation set by z_velocity
    (in units of m/s) to perturb their orbits above and below the plane.
    
    Arguments
    ---------
        num_of_particles : int
            The total number of particles to create with the first particle
            being a solar-mass star
    
        mass_ratio : float
            The ratio of the mass of each planetesimal to the mass of the
            central star.
    
        z_velocity : float
            z-axis velocity standard deviation
    
    Returns
    -------
        masses, positions, velocities :
            masses 1D np.array whose shape is (nParticles)
            positions 2D np.array whose shape is (nParticles, nDimensions)
            velocities 2D np.array whose shape is (nParticles, nDimensions)
